ERR_001.title: Sensor Malfunction

root_causes.diagnosis: Visual inspection of proximity sensors (usually 4-6 sensors around robot body). Look for dust, oil film, plastic film, or fingerprints on lens surface. Sensor lens should be clear and shiny.
advanced_steps: STEP 1 - LOCATE SENSORS: Find all proximity sensors (typically black circular units 2-3cm diameter on robot sides/front/back)
STEP 2 - VISUAL CHECK: Use flashlight to inspect each sensor lens for contamination
STEP 3 - CLEAN GENTLY: Dampen microfiber cloth with isopropyl alcohol (NOT water)
STEP 4 - WIPE LENS: Gently wipe lens in circular motion, don't press hard
STEP 5 - DRY: Let air dry 30 seconds or use dry cloth
STEP 6 - BLOW DEBRIS: Use compressed air to remove particles from sensor housing (hold can upright, 15cm distance)
STEP 7 - TEST: Power on robot, wave hand 5-20cm from sensor - LED should blink or robot should respond
STEP 8 - REPEAT: Clean all sensors (front, back, left, right sides)
EXPECTED RESULT: Sensor LED blinks when object detected, robot navigates smoothly without random stops
root_causes.prevention: Clean sensors weekly in dusty environments, install protective covers if available

root_causes.diagnosis: Trace sensor cable from sensor unit to main control board. Check for loose connectors (should click firmly), pinched cables, cuts, or exposed wires.
advanced_steps: STEP 1 - POWER OFF: Completely power down robot and engage emergency stop
STEP 2 - LOCATE CABLE: Follow cable from faulty sensor to connection point (usually at robot base or control box)
STEP 3 - INSPECT CONNECTOR: Check connector for bent pins, corrosion, or foreign material
STEP 4 - CHECK CABLE PATH: Look for pinch points, sharp bends (radius should be >2cm), or cable rubbing against metal
STEP 5 - RESEAT CONNECTOR: Unplug connector, inspect pins, firmly reinsert until you hear/feel click
STEP 6 - SECURE CABLE: Ensure cable is properly routed and secured with cable ties, not hanging loose
STEP 7 - WIGGLE TEST: Gently move cable while monitoring - if loose connection, will see intermittent contact
STEP 8 - POWER TEST: Turn on robot, test sensor function before resuming operations
IF DAMAGED CABLE FOUND: Mark location with tape, document with photo, call technician - cable replacement requires proper routing and connector crimping
root_causes.prevention: Inspect cables monthly, ensure proper cable management, avoid sharp bends

root_causes.diagnosis: Occurs near high-power electrical equipment, wireless transmitters, or metal structures. Test by moving robot to different area - if error disappears, it's EMI.
advanced_steps: STEP 1 - IDENTIFY PATTERN: Note where errors occur (near forklifts, metal shelving, charging stations, wireless routers)
STEP 2 - TEST ELSEWHERE: Move robot to open area away from equipment - if sensors work, it's EMI
STEP 3 - CHECK NEARBY: Look for: welding equipment, large motors, radio transmitters, metal detectors, high-voltage cables
STEP 4 - DOCUMENT: Mark problematic zones on warehouse map
STEP 5 - SHORT TERM: Route robots around problematic areas, adjust patrol paths
STEP 6 - LONG TERM: Contact technician for sensor shielding upgrade or EMI filtering installation
COMMON EMI SOURCES: Arc welders (25m radius), industrial microwaves (10m), high-power WiFi (5m), AC motors >50HP (15m)
root_causes.prevention: Keep robots 10m+ from high-power equipment, install EMI shields on sensors

root_causes.diagnosis: After cleaning and cable check, if sensor still doesn't work, it's likely hardware failure. Sensor life expectancy: 3-5 years.
advanced_steps: CONFIRM OTHER CAUSES ELIMINATED: Must have tried cleaning, cable reseating, and EMI testing first
CHECK SENSOR AGE: Look for manufacturing date on sensor or check maintenance logs (sensors typically last 3-5 years)
VISUAL DAMAGE CHECK: Look for cracks, burned components, water damage, impact damage
COMPARE TO WORKING SENSOR: Check if other sensors on same robot work - helps rule out power supply issue
TECHNICIAN REQUIRED: Hardware replacement needs: proper sensor calibration, bracket mounting, cable routing, system recalibration
TYPICAL PARTS: Sensor unit cost $150-300, Installation 30-60 min, Includes calibration
TEMPORARY WORKAROUND: If robot has multiple redundant sensors, technician may temporarily disable failed one and adjust sensitivity on remaining sensors
root_causes.prevention: Regular maintenance, avoid physical impacts, protect from water/chemicals

common_operator_questions.question: I cleaned the sensor but error still appears
common_operator_questions.answer: If cleaning didn't work: 1) Check the sensor cable connection - unplug and firmly reseat it. 2) Test in a different warehouse area (might be EMI). 3) Check if other sensors work (could be power supply issue). 4) Look for visible damage to sensor unit. If all these check out, sensor hardware has likely failed and needs technician replacement (typical cost $150-300, takes 30-60 minutes).

common_operator_questions.question: How do I know which sensor is faulty?
common_operator_questions.answer: Robot typically has 4-6 sensors (front, back, left, right, sometimes top/bottom). To identify faulty one: 1) Check robot error display - may show 'Sensor 1', 'Front Sensor', etc. 2) Wave hand near each sensor individually - working sensors will trigger response (LED blink or robot stops). 3) Look for sensor with no LED activity. 4) Check maintenance panel in robot software - usually shows sensor status individually with PASS/FAIL indicators.

common_operator_questions.question: Can robot operate with one sensor not working?
common_operator_questions.answer: NO - do not operate robot with faulty sensor. Reasons: 1) Safety hazard - robot can't detect obstacles on that side, may collide with people/equipment. 2) Navigation issues - robot uses all sensors for positioning, missing data causes erratic movement. 3) Liability - company is responsible for accidents if operating with known sensor fault. 4) May damage other components trying to compensate. Keep robot offline until repaired.

common_operator_questions.question: What causes sensors to fail frequently?
common_operator_questions.answer: Common causes of repeated sensor failures: 1) DUSTY ENVIRONMENT - implement more frequent cleaning schedule (weekly instead of monthly). 2) CHEMICAL EXPOSURE - certain cleaning agents damage sensor lens, use only approved cleaners. 3) PHYSICAL IMPACTS - robot hitting shelving/walls, install protective bumpers. 4) MOISTURE - humidity or water spray, install protective covers. 5) VIBRATION - mounting screws loose, check/tighten monthly. 6) EMI - near electrical equipment, install EMI shielding. Address root environmental cause, not just replace sensors repeatedly.

common_operator_questions.question: How often should sensors be cleaned?
common_operator_questions.answer: NORMAL WAREHOUSE: Monthly. DUSTY/INDUSTRIAL: Weekly. HIGH-DUST (concrete cutting, sanding): Every 2-3 days. FOOD/PHARMA (clean rooms): Monthly is usually sufficient. OUTDOOR ROBOTS: After rain or weekly. You can tell sensors need cleaning when: 1) Robot pauses more frequently. 2) Visible dust/film on lens. 3) Error logs show increasing sensor-related issues. 4) LED response seems delayed. Set reminders based on your environment - preventive cleaning is much faster than troubleshooting failures.

technical_specifications.cleaning_solution: 70% Isopropyl alcohol only - NO water, acetone, or harsh chemicals

safety_warnings: CRITICAL: Always power off robot before touching sensors or cables
Do not use water to clean sensors - use isopropyl alcohol only
Never operate robot with known faulty sensor - creates collision hazard
When cleaning, avoid spraying liquid directly on sensor - may enter housing
Do not touch sensor lens with bare hands - oils from skin reduce performance
escalation_criteria: Cable damaged or connector has bent pins
Sensor hardware physically damaged (cracks, burn marks)
Error persists after all basic troubleshooting
preventive_maintenance: Clean sensors monthly (weekly in dusty environments)
Check sensor response quarterly (wave hand test)
Review error logs monthly for increasing sensor issues
Document cleaning dates in maintenance log

ERR_002.title: Low Battery Critical

root_causes.diagnosis: This is normal operation - battery simply needs recharging. Robot should auto-navigate to charging station.
advanced_steps: STEP 1 - VERIFY AUTO-CHARGE: Robot should automatically navigate to nearest available charging dock
STEP 2 - CLEAR PATH: Ensure path to charging station is clear of obstacles, pallets, or people
STEP 3 - CHECK DOCK: Confirm charging dock power is on (usually has green LED indicator)
STEP 4 - MONITOR APPROACH: Watch robot navigate to dock - should slow down and align carefully
STEP 5 - CONFIRM CONNECTION: Robot should dock with contacts aligned, hear 'click' sound
STEP 6 - CHARGING INDICATOR: Look for charging status - LED turns orange/red, battery icon shows lightning bolt
STEP 7 - WAIT 15 MINUTES: Battery should reach 20% in 15-20 minutes (fast charge mode)
STEP 8 - FULL CHARGE: Complete charge to 100% takes 60-90 minutes depending on battery size
NORMAL CHARGE RATE: 1-1.5% per minute in fast charge mode, 0.5-0.8% in normal mode
IF CHARGING SLOWER: Check contact points for corrosion, verify dock output voltage (should be 48-52V DC)
root_causes.prevention: Schedule charging during low-activity periods, don't wait until <10%

root_causes.diagnosis: Robot reaches dock but battery doesn't charge or charges very slowly (<0.3% per minute). Issue is with dock, not robot.
advanced_steps: STEP 1 - CHECK DOCK POWER: Verify dock power cable is plugged in and outlet has power (test with multimeter or plug in phone charger)
STEP 2 - DOCK LED STATUS: Green = ready, Orange = charging in progress, Red = fault, Off = no power
STEP 3 - INSPECT CONTACTS: Look at charging contacts on both robot and dock
STEP 4 - CONTACT CLEANING: Use contact cleaner spray or isopropyl alcohol on cloth to clean contacts on both sides
STEP 5 - CHECK ALIGNMENT: Contacts should align perfectly when docked - even 2-3mm misalignment prevents charging
STEP 6 - VOLTAGE TEST (if trained): Measure dock output voltage with multimeter - should be 48-52V DC when robot not connected
STEP 7 - TEST OTHER ROBOT: If another robot charges fine on same dock, issue is with first robot's charging port
STEP 8 - TEST OTHER DOCK: If robot charges fine on different dock, issue is with first dock
STEP 9 - CIRCUIT BREAKER: Check facility breaker panel - charging dock circuits sometimes trip (usually 20A breakers)
STEP 10 - RESET DOCK: Power cycle dock (unplug 30 seconds, plug back in) then retry
IF DOCK FAULTY: Call maintenance - typical issues are power supply failure ($200-500) or contact spring wear ($50-100)
root_causes.prevention: Clean dock contacts monthly, test dock voltage quarterly, keep dock area dry

root_causes.diagnosis: Normal battery aging - capacity decreases over time. Lithium batteries lose ~20% capacity after 2-3 years of daily use.
advanced_steps: STEP 1 - CHECK BATTERY AGE: Look for manufacturing date sticker on battery or check installation records
STEP 2 - CAPACITY TEST: Fully charge battery, run robot continuously, measure how long until 20%
STEP 3 - COMPARE TO BASELINE: New battery should run 6-8 hours continuous operation, degraded battery 4-5 hours
STEP 4 - VOLTAGE SAG TEST: Check battery voltage under load vs idle - >5V drop indicates aging cells
STEP 5 - REVIEW LOGS: Check maintenance software for battery health score (usually 0-100%, <70% needs replacement)
STEP 6 - CYCLE COUNT: Batteries rated for 1000-1500 charge cycles, after that capacity drops significantly
BATTERY LIFESPAN FACTORS:
- DAILY USE: 2-3 years typical
- FREQUENT DEEP DISCHARGE: Reduces life 20-30%
- HIGH TEMPERATURE (>30C): Reduces life 30-40%
- KEPT AT 100% ALWAYS: Reduces life 10-20%
OPTIMAL: Keep battery 40-80% when not in use, avoid deep discharge below 10%
STEP 7 - REPLACEMENT NEEDED: If battery <70% capacity or >3 years old with performance issues
COST: Battery replacement $800-2000 depending on size, takes 1-2 hours labor
root_causes.prevention: Avoid deep discharge, keep temperature moderate, replace batteries proactively after 3 years

root_causes.cause: Robot Overworked / Task Load Too High
symptoms: Battery drains faster on certain days
Drains quickly when carrying heavy loads
Fine when idle but drops fast when working
root_causes.diagnosis: Robot assigned too many tasks or carrying loads beyond optimal range, causing excessive power consumption.
advanced_steps: STEP 1 - REVIEW TASK LOG: Check how many tasks assigned vs completed, look for increasing backlog
STEP 2 - CHECK PAYLOAD: Review typical weights carried - should be within 70% of max capacity for efficient operation
STEP 3 - ANALYZE ROUTES: Long routes with many turns consume more power than straight paths
STEP 4 - MONITOR SPEED: Robot running at max speed constantly uses 30-40% more battery than moderate speed
STEP 5 - CHECK ACCELERATION: Frequent start/stop cycles drain battery faster than smooth continuous movement
STEP 6 - FLOOR CONDITION: Rough floors, inclines, or obstacles force robot to work harder
POWER CONSUMPTION RATES:
- IDLE: 50-80W
- MOVING EMPTY: 150-250W
- MOVING WITH 50% LOAD: 250-350W
- MOVING WITH MAX LOAD: 400-500W
- CLIMBING 5° RAMP: +100W
STEP 7 - OPTIMIZE: Reduce max speed 10-20%, limit acceleration, optimize routes, balance load across fleet
STEP 8 - ADD CHARGING BREAKS: If shifts >8 hours, schedule 15-min charge breaks at 40-50% battery
root_causes.prevention: Balance workload, optimize routes, avoid overloading, schedule mid-shift charge breaks

common_operator_questions.question: How long does charging take?
common_operator_questions.answer: QUICK CHARGE (0-20%): 15-20 minutes. HALF CHARGE (0-50%): 35-45 minutes. FULL CHARGE (0-100%): 60-90 minutes. FAST CHARGING: Some docks support fast charge to 80% in 40 minutes, but last 20% always takes longer (battery chemistry limits). You'll typically see charge rates of 1-1.5% per minute up to 80%, then drops to 0.3-0.5% per minute for final 20%. Many warehouses operate on 'opportunity charging' - robot charges whenever idle for >10 minutes, doesn't need full 100%.

common_operator_questions.question: Robot goes to charge but battery still shows low
common_operator_questions.answer: This indicates charging system fault, not normal operation. Check: 1) CHARGING INDICATOR - Should see orange/red LED and lightning bolt icon within 2 minutes of docking. If not, not actually charging. 2) CONTACT ALIGNMENT - Undock and redock robot, listen for 'click' sound. 3) CLEAN CONTACTS - Corrosion or dirt prevents electrical connection. 4) TEST OTHER DOCK - If works on different dock, original dock is faulty. 5) CHECK DOCK POWER - Verify dock has power (green LED). If all checks pass but still no charge, likely issue with robot's charging circuit - requires technician.

common_operator_questions.question: Is it bad to charge battery frequently?
common_operator_questions.answer: NO - modern lithium batteries don't have 'memory effect' and actually prefer frequent partial charges over deep discharge. BEST PRACTICE: Charge whenever robot is idle for >10 minutes, even if battery is 60-70%. AVOID: Letting battery drop below 10% regularly - this reduces battery lifespan by 20-30%. MYTH: 'Must fully discharge before charging' - this applied to old NiCad batteries, NOT lithium. OPTIMAL: Keep battery between 40-80% for longest lifespan, though 20-90% is acceptable for daily ops.

common_operator_questions.question: Why does battery percentage jump around?
common_operator_questions.answer: This is normal for lithium batteries due to voltage-based estimation. UNDER LOAD: Battery voltage drops, percentage may show lower. IDLE: Voltage recovers, percentage may show higher. COLD: Battery shows lower percentage than actual (voltage temporarily depressed). AFTER CHARGE: May show 100% but drop to 95% after 5 minutes (surface charge dissipates). MOST ACCURATE: Reading after robot has been idle for 5+ minutes. If percentage jumps wildly (like 50% to 20% in 1 minute), this indicates failing battery cells - needs technician diagnosis with proper battery analyzer.

common_operator_questions.question: Can I manually push robot to charging dock?
common_operator_questions.answer: YES but with precautions: 1) ENGAGE MANUAL MODE - Put robot in manual push mode first (usually button on robot or remote). 2) EMERGENCY STOP - Press emergency stop button before pushing. 3) PUSH GENTLY - Robot weighs 200-500 kg, don't strain yourself. 4) STRAIGHT PUSH - Push from behind, not from sides (damages wheels). 5) ALIGN CAREFULLY - Charging requires precise alignment, use painted markers on floor. 6) DISENGAGE MANUAL - Turn off manual mode after docking. DON'T PUSH if: Robot has brakes engaged and won't release, payload on robot (unload first), no manual mode button found (call technician).

technical_specifications.typical_lifespan: 2-3 years daily use, 4-5 years moderate use

safety_warnings: DO NOT attempt to open battery compartment - high voltage hazard
Keep battery dry - water + lithium = fire risk
If battery smells burnt or swells, evacuate area and call fire department
Never force charging contacts together - alignment must be natural
Damaged batteries can catch fire - if dropped or impacted, call technician
escalation_criteria: Battery age over 3 years with performance issues
Battery won't charge on any dock
Unusual smells or heat from battery
preventive_maintenance: Review battery health scores in software weekly
